llm_text: I still lean toward agreeing that adult children have a duty to care for ill parents when they’re realistically able — it feels like part of the circle of life and what you’d hope someone would do for you. That said, real limits (abuse, distance, low-pay restaurant work, or burnout) can make it impossible, and duty shouldn’t mean doing it alone: share responsibility, use paid help when needed, set boundaries, and plan practically.

text: I believe it is the child's duty to take care of ill parents.  If they are adults and able to do it, they should.  If the parents raised the child in a loving home, they deserve to be taken care of.
llm_text: I still agree — when grown children are able, caring for ill parents is a duty and can be one of the most meaningful things you do (it was for me with my mom). That said, my conversations reinforced that it isn’t automatic: abuse, estrangement, distance, or financial and work constraints can make it impossible, and it’s important to set boundaries, use paid or community supports, and protect your own health.

text: We should try to look after the people who once looked after us and pass that moral duty on to future generations.  If we do not care for our parents, how can we expect our children to care for us?
llm_text: I disagree — it shouldn’t be an automatic, unquestioned duty. When adult children are physically and financially able and the relationship is healthy, honoring and helping parents is the right and often scripture-supported thing to do, but abuse, estrangement, or genuine inability change the equation and require boundaries, planning, and community or paid support.
